notes.short: Heavens, earth, grain, Jezreel: a chain of answers
notes.about: Each line takes up the one before it: the LORD answers the heavens, the heavens the earth, the earth the grain, new wine and oil, and these answer Jezreel. Every link hangs on the one above it and the highest on God, so the blessing comes down step by step to His people.

lines.words: I will respond to the heavens,
and they will respond to the earth.
And the earth will respond to the grain, to the new wine and oil,
and they will respond to Jezreel.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists these verses under Climax: each in its turn hears and cries out to the next, up to Jehovah. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) sees all things, from lowest to highest, bound together, each depending on the one beyond and the highest on God. Henry sees second causes linked as a chain, all hanging on God, the grain crying to the earth, the earth to the heavens, the heavens to God.
notes.limit: The answers come down from God to His people; the chain can also be read upward, each asking the one above it, from Jezreel up to the LORD.

cites.quote: are represented as hearing, and in their turn, crying out to the Earth to bring them forth: the Earth, in its turn, is represented as hearing them, and crying out to the heavens to send rain and heat and light and air; and these in their turn hear, and cry out to Jehovah, the giver of all
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: And, as an image of love, all, from lowest to highest, are bound together, each depending on the ministry of that beyond it, and the highest on God. At each link, the chain might have been broken; but God who knit their services together, and had before withheld the rain, and made the earth barren, and laid waste the trees, now made each to supply the other
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: See here the coherence of second causes with one another, as links in a chain, and the necessary dependence they all have upon God, the first Cause. … the corn cries to the earth, the earth to the heavens, the heavens to God, and all that they may supply them.

notes.about: The LORD says “I will respond” twice. Saying it twice makes the promise firm, so that a people worn down by famine under judgment, who might have lost hope, could rely on it.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.words: I will respond—” declares the LORD— “I will respond
figure.means: the LORD's promise to answer, made firm by being said twice

original.note: In Hebrew the verb is anah, to answer, the same verb used for every answer that follows.

notes.evidence: Bullinger names the doubled “I will hear” as Epizeuxis, one of the figures heaped together here to express the fulness of Israel's coming blessing. Clarke says the sentence is repeated to show how fully the Almighty had resolved it and how surely they might rely on it; Calvin says the repetition is not needless, for by it God raises up a people worn down by famine.

cites.quote: Thus the figures Epizeuxis (“I will hear”), Polysyndeton , Climax , and Prosopopœia are heaped together to express the coming fulness of Israel’s blessing.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: I will hear, saith the Lord - The sentence is repeated, to show how fully the thing was determined by the Almighty, and how implicitly they might depend on the Divine promise.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: I will hear, he says, or I will answer, (ענה, one, means to answer, but it is here equivalent to hear,) … The repetition is not superfluous; for the Israelites had been for some time consumed by famine … They might hence have thought that there was now no hope; but God here raises them up, I will hear, I will hear, he says

notes.short: The heavens hear the earth and answer it
notes.about: The heavens are spoken of as a person who hears and answers: when the earth seems to ask for rain, the heavens answer it. Behind them the LORD answers the heavens, so nothing in nature gives its gifts to His people without His bidding.

figure.name: Personification
figure.part: Human actions attributed to inanimate things
figure.words: they will respond to the earth
figure.means: the heavens give the earth the rain it needs, as one person answers another who asks

notes.evidence: Bullinger names Prosopopoeia here: grain, wine and oil, the earth and the heavens are represented as hearing and crying out in turn. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it a prosopopeia, the heaven praying to God and then fulfilling the earth's desires. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls it personification, the skies hearing the earth beg for rain. Clarke: the earth seems to plead for rain.

cites.quote: these, by the beautiful figure of Prosopopœia … are represented as hearing, and in their turn, crying out to the Earth to bring them forth: the Earth, in its turn, is represented as hearing them, and crying out to the heavens to send rain and heat and light and air; and these in their turn hear, and cry out to Jehovah
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: By a prosopopeia, the prophet represents the heaven as praying to God, to allow it to give to the earth that which is requisite to ensure its fertility; whereupon the heaven fulfils the desires of the earth, and the earth yields its produce to the nation.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: heavens . . . hear the earth--personification. However many be the intermediate instruments, God is the Great First Cause of all nature's phenomena. … and that the skies again would hearken to the earth begging for a supply of the rain it requires
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: I will hear the heavens - The visible heavens, the atmosphere, where vapours are collected. The clouds, when they wish to deposit their fertilizing showers upon the earth. They shall hear the earth - When it seems to supplicate for rain.

notes.short: What shall I do with you, Ephraim, Judah?
notes.about: The second line says the first again by repeating its question: what shall I do with you, O Ephraim, O Judah.

lines.words: What shall I do with you, O Ephraim?
What shall I do with you, O Judah?

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse among parallel lines that are made by repeating part of the first line.

cites.quote: Parallels are also sometimes formed by a repetition of part of the first sentence:

notes.short: A prayer that stops short: “what will You give?”
notes.about: The prophet begins a prayer, “Give them, O LORD,” and stops short to ask, “what will You give?” Only then does he name wombs that miscarry and breasts that dry up. Two of the writers read the broken-off words as a sign of how deeply the judgment coming on Ephraim moves him.

figure.name: Aposiopesis
figure.means: a prayer begun and broken off, as if the prophet cannot say what to ask, before he names barrenness

original.note: In Hebrew the question “what will You give?” is two words, mah titten, set into the prayer between two cries of ten, “give.”

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Hosea 9:14 under Aposiopesis: the prophet, as though he cannot conceive the punishment deserved, breaks off and returns to the thought of verse 11. Clarke says he began to intercede and the Spirit interrupted his petition. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) sees the inserted question as a mark of excited speech. Benson says the prophet speaks greatly agitated and at a loss what to say.
notes.limit: The writers differ on why he stops: one hears a plea for mercy cut short by God's Spirit, another holy indignation calling for the judgment.

cites.quote: As though unable to conceive the punishment deserved, the Prophet breaks off and goes back to the thought of verse 11.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The prophet, seeing the evils that were likely to fall upon his countrymen, begins to make intercession for them; but when he had formed the first part of his petition, "Give them, O Lord!" the prophetic light discovered to him that the petition would not be answered ... Then changing his petition, which the Divine Spirit had interrupted, by signifying that he must not proceed in his request
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In Hos 9:14 the threat rises into an appeal to God to execute the threatened punishment. The excited style of the language is indicated in the interpolated mah-titteen (what wilt Thou give?). The words do not contain an intercessory prayer on the part of the prophet ... but are expressive of holy indignation at the deep corruption of the people.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The prophet here speaks as one greatly agitated, and at a loss what to say upon what he had just heard

notes.short: “O Israel”: God cries out over Israel's ruin
notes.about: God's words come as a cry, not a bare statement: “You are destroyed, O Israel, because you are against Me.” They burst out from feeling over the ruin Israel brought on itself by turning against the One who was its helper.

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.means: God's strong feeling over the ruin Israel brought on itself by turning against Him, its helper

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Hosea 13:9 under Ecphonesis, words that burst out from feeling.

cites.quote: So that Ecphonesis is an outburst of words, prompted by emotion, and is not used as though any reply were expected. ... Hos 13:9. -“O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself; but in me is thine help.”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.about: Sheol is named in the first line and the last, and Death in the two lines between: the LORD will ransom them and redeem them, then asks where the plagues of Death and the sting of Sheol are.

lines.words: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol;
I will redeem them from Death.
Where, O Death, are your plagues?
Where, O Sheol, is your sting?

notes.evidence: Jebb gives the verse as an example of what he calls the introverted parallelism, in which, he says, the first and last lines are parallel, and so are the second and the next to last.

cites.quote: There are stanzas so constructed, that, whatever be the number of lines, the first line shall be parallel with the last; the second with the penultimate; and so throughout, in an order that looks inward, or, to borrow a military phrase, from flanks to centre. This may be called the introverted parallelism
cites.read: the 1820 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/sacredliterature00jebb
